title: Area and Arc Length in Polar Coordinates
short: Area and Arc Length in Polar Coordinates
lead: The definite integral gives areas and arc lengths in polar coordinates too. This section adds up sectors of circles to find the area of a region bounded by a polar curve, finds the area between two polar curves, and measures the arc length of a polar curve.
objectives: Apply the formula for area of a region in polar coordinates.
Determine the arc length of a polar curve.
summary_html:
• The area of a region in polar coordinates defined by the equation $r=\kf(\ktheta )$ with $\alpha \le \ktheta \le β$ is given by the integral $\kA=\frac{1}{2}{\int_{\alpha}^{β}[\kf(\ktheta )] }^{2}d\theta .$
  • To find the area between two curves in the polar coordinate system, first find the points of intersection, then subtract the corresponding areas.
  • The arc length of a polar curve defined by the equation $r=\kf(\ktheta )$ with $\alpha \le \ktheta \le β$ is given by the integral $\kL=\int_{\alpha}^{β}\sqrt{{[\kf(\ktheta )]}^{2}+{[\kfprime(\ktheta )]}^{2}}d\theta =\int_{\alpha}^{β}\sqrt{r^{2}+{(\frac{dr}{d\theta})}^{2}}d\theta .$

exercises.prompt: Show that the curve $r=\sin \theta \;\tan \theta$ (called a cissoid of Diocles) has the line $x=1$ as a vertical asymptote.

answer.solution: Write the curve parametrically: $x=r\cos \theta =\sin \theta \tan \theta \cos \theta ={\sin }^{2}\theta$ and $y=r\sin \theta ={\sin }^{2}\theta \tan \theta .$ As $\theta \to \frac{\pi}{2}$ from either side, $x={\sin }^{2}\theta \to 1$ while $\tan \theta$ becomes unbounded, so $|y|\to \infty .$ The points of the curve therefore approach the vertical line $x=1,$ going up as $\theta \to \frac{\pi}{2}^{-}$ and down as $\theta \to \frac{\pi}{2}^{+};$ and since $x={\sin }^{2}\theta \lt 1$ wherever $y$ is defined, the curve never reaches it. So $x=1$ is a vertical asymptote.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

The arc length of the spiral given by $r=\frac{\theta}{2}$ for $0\le \theta \le 3\pi$ is $\frac{9}{4}{\pi}^{3}.$

answer.solution: False. By Equation 11.10 with $r=\frac{\theta}{2}$ and $\frac{dr}{d\theta}=\frac{1}{2},$ $L=\int_0^{3\pi}\sqrt{\frac{{\theta}^{2}}{4}+\frac{1}{4}}\;d\theta =\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{3\pi}\sqrt{{\theta}^{2}+1}\;d\theta \approx 23.0.$ The value $\frac{9}{4}{\pi}^{3}\approx 69.8$ is $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{3\pi}{\theta}^{2}\,d\theta ,$ which is neither the length nor the area swept, $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{3\pi}\frac{{\theta}^{2}}{4}d\theta =\frac{9}{8}{\pi}^{3}.$

assumes.text: A sector with central angle $\ktheta$ radians is the fraction $\frac{\ktheta}{2\pi}$ of its circle.
The $i$th sector has central angle $\Delta \ktheta$ and radius $r_{i}=\kf({\ktheta}_{i}).$
The sectors together approximate the region, and the approximation becomes exact as $n\to \infty .$
A Riemann sum $\sum g({\ktheta}_{i})\Delta \ktheta$ approaches $\int_{\alpha}^{\beta }g(\ktheta )d\theta$ as $n\to \infty .$
